text: Start with a = 2. A Value holds one number (data) and one gradient (grad), which is still zero.
Add b = -3. Inputs are plain Values; no operation connects them yet.
Multiply: mul = a × b = -6. The new node remembers its two operands, so the graph now has edges.
Add the third input: c = 10.
Add: d = a × b + c = 4. This root node is the expression we will differentiate.
Backward pass: d.grad = 1. Then mul.grad = 1 and c.grad = 1; the chain rule gives a.grad = b = -3 and b.grad = a = 2.
We already have d = a × b + c = 4. Backward starts at the output and walks the graph in reverse topological order, accumulating each node’s grad.
Only operations are numbered: ① + must run before ② ×. The × node’s gradient has to be complete before it can pass anything back to a and b — that is the reverse topological order.
Seed the output: d.grad = 1 (∂d/∂d). Every other grad is still zero.
Process ① +: d.grad = 1 flows back along both edges. The local derivatives are ∂d/∂mul = 1 and ∂d/∂c = 1, so mul.grad = 1 and c.grad = 1.
Process ② ×: mul.grad = 1 flows to a and b. The local derivatives are ∂mul/∂a = b = -3 and ∂mul/∂b = a = 2, so a.grad = 1 × -3 = -3 and b.grad = 1 × 2 = 2.
Done. Chain rule along a → mul → d: ∂d/∂a = ∂d/∂mul · ∂mul/∂a = 1 · b = -3. Reverse topological order made mul.grad complete before it was used.
A neuron computes y = tanh(w · x + b) with three inputs. Start with the inputs x, the weights w, and the bias b — all plain Values.
Multiply each weight by its input: p1 = w1 × x1 = 0.5, p2 = w2 × x2 = -0.5, p3 = w3 × x3 = -2.
Sum the products and add the bias: z = (0.5 + -0.5) + -2 + 2.5 = 0.5.
Squash with tanh: y = tanh(0.5) = 0.46. Forward pass done — now send the gradient back.

Backward starts at the output: y.grad = 1 (∂y/∂y). Operations are numbered in reverse topological order; each one runs only after every node that consumes its result. The weight gradients are still zero.
Process tanh: ∂y/∂z = 1 − y² = 0.79. Chain rule: z.grad = y.grad × 0.79 = 0.79.
Process +: z.grad splits equally into dot2 and b because both local derivatives are 1. dot2.grad = b.grad = 0.79.
Process +: dot2.grad splits into dot1 and p3; both local derivatives are 1.
Process +: dot1.grad splits into p1 and p2; both local derivatives are 1.
Process ×: p1.grad flows into w1 and x1. ∂p1/∂w1 = x1 = 1, so w1.grad = 1 × 0.79 = 0.79; ∂p1/∂x1 = w1 = 0.5, so x1.grad = 0.5 × 0.79 = 0.39.
All three weight gradients: w1 = 0.79, w2 = 0.39, w3 = -0.79. Gradient descent would subtract a small multiple of each (ticket 3); no training loop here.
The same neuron as scene 3: y = tanh(w · x + b). This time we know the answer we want: a target t = 1. The parameters w and b are the Values that training will change.
Forward pass: z = 0.5, so y = tanh(0.5) = 0.46. The prediction is a Value, built out of Values.
Measure the error: loss = (y − t)² = (0.46 − 1)² = 0.29. A bigger miss gives a bigger loss.
Backward starts at the loss: loss.grad = 1. Operations run in reverse topological order, so each node receives every contribution before it passes its gradient on.
Differentiate the square: ∂loss/∂diff = 2 × diff = -1.08, so diff.grad = -1.08.
Differentiate the subtraction: ∂diff/∂y = 1 and ∂diff/∂t = −1, so y.grad = -1.08 and t.grad = 1.08. The target is an input, not a parameter.
Through tanh: ∂y/∂z = 1 − y² = 0.79, so z.grad = y.grad × 0.79 = -0.85.
Through the bias add: z.grad splits equally into dot2 and b, so each gets -0.85.
Through the second add: dot2.grad splits into dot1 and p3 (both local derivatives are 1).
Through the first add: dot1.grad splits into p1 and p2 (both local derivatives are 1).
Through the first product: w1.grad = x1 × p1.grad = 1 × -0.85 = 0; x1 is an input, so its gradient stops here.
Through the second product: w2.grad = x2 × p2.grad = 0.5 × -0.85 = 0.
Through the third product: w3.grad = x3 × p3.grad = -1 × -0.85 = 0. All parameter gradients are now complete.
Gradient descent takes one step along the negative gradient: p ← p − lr · g with lr = 0.1. Each parameter annotation shows −g and the new data; the table lists every weight before and after.

After one update the loss fell from 0.29 to 0.12. w₁ moved +0.08 because its gradient was -0.85. Gradients are cleared with zeroGrad() before the next forward pass. Scene 5 repeats this loop until the network learns.
Before training: the weights are random, so the loss is 1.32 and the dashed boundary misclassifies points. The loop will now run forward → loss → backward → step.
